newsitem.title: ZAIRE: Zaire protests spread to remote Kisangani.
newsitem.headline: Zaire protests spread to remote Kisangani.

text.p: Hundreds of students burned Rwandan-owned property in the northeastern Zaire town of Kisangani on Wednesday as protests against government handling of a Tutsi rebellion in the east spread.

Soldiers have been pouring into the riverside town from the war front on the Rwandan and Burundian border where the army has lost ground to ethnic-Tutsi rebels whom Zaire says are backed by Tutsi-led Rwanda.

"The government has not done enough to help the army drive out the Rwandan invaders," yelled one angry student, targeting the government led by part-Tutsi Prime Minister Kengo wa Dondo. "The Rwandans have to go, and so does the government."
Outside one Rwandan-owned building near the centre of the usually tranquil city, a pile of belongings burned. The occupants had fled.
Witnesses said hundreds of protesters took part. Similar protests in the capital Kinshasa put hundreds of Tutsis to flight. Most went to neighbouring Congo.
Dozens of uniformed soldiers have made their way to Kisangani from the war front. Commandeered aid vehicles cruise the streets.

Kisangani, with the appearance of an overgrown village, now has a population of 500,000 people and is the last major outpost before the hills and jungle that could conceal one of Africa's worst humanitarian disasters.
Even contact with missionary radio has been lost with many of the villages on the 500-km road from the rebel-held refugee town of Goma. Kinshasa is twice as far away to the south west.
The Tutsi revolt has put to flight over a million Hutu refugees from Rwanda and Burundi and several hundred thousand Zaireans.
Many of the Hutus fled Rwanda in 1994, fearing reprisals or a flare-up in civil war after Hutu hardliners massacred up to a million Tutsis there.
Aid agencies pulled out of Zaire last weekend after the rebels advanced through Zaire's eastern refugee provinces of North and South Kivu and fighting made their work impossible.
The refugees have also taken flight and no one has any clear idea where they are.

"The best information we have is from Lubutu, over 200 km (120 miles) away. Brothers and sisters there say they are in desperate need of medical supplies," said Jose des Chartes Menga, chairman of a local human rights group. "An outbreak of diarrhoea has already begun among local people."
Aid workers, stuck outside Zaire, fear outbreaks of cholera, dysentery and other diseases which killed around 50,000 people in squalid camps during the 1994 refugee exodus from Rwanda.
Witnesses say refugees and displaced people are also having to contend with Zaire's rag-tag army, whose soldiers are notoriously ill-disciplined and predatory, often living off the local population.
"All along the road, people have been forced into the bush. They are running not just from the Rwandans but from retreating soldiers as well," said a foreign businessman who had escaped from Bukavu.
Diamond dealers, many of them Lebanese, have closed their shops in Kisangani in anticipation of trouble.
Businessmen say food prices are soaring in the city as access to surrounding areas is cut off. A 50 kilo sack of rice costs $50 compared to $30 a few days ago.
